does-my-outfit-look-good.body_html:
Your outfit probably looks good if it fits the way the pieces were designed to, the colors and shapes work together, it suits where you're going, and you feel comfortable in it. If you're asking "does my outfit look good?", the fastest way to find out is to check those things one at a time instead of judging the whole look at once. This guide gives you a fair way to look at yourself, a 7-point checklist, and quick fixes for the most common problems.

Start with what "good" actually means

"Does it look good?" is really several questions bundled together. Separating them makes the answer much easier to find.

Three separate questions

  • Does it fit? Are the garments sitting where they should, without pulling, gaping or swamping you?
  • Does it work together? Do the colors, textures and shapes look like one outfit rather than separate pieces?
  • Does it suit the occasion? Is the formality right for the place, the people and the weather?

An outfit can pass one test and fail another. A well-fitted suit is wrong for a beach wedding, and a perfectly coordinated outfit is still a bad choice if the trousers dig in when you sit down.

Comfort and feeling like yourself count too

If you keep tugging at a hem or adjusting a neckline, it shows in how you carry yourself. An outfit that is slightly less "perfect" on paper but that you feel at ease in often looks better in real life. Treat comfort as part of the check, not an afterthought.

Set up a fair check: mirror test and photo test

A quick glance in a hallway mirror hides a lot. A slightly more careful setup gives you a much more honest read.

Full-length mirror, good light, shoes on

Put on the shoes you'll actually wear, stand a few steps back from a full-length mirror, and use daylight or bright, even light. Judging the outfit without shoes changes the proportions of trousers, skirts and dresses, so don't skip them.

Take a head-to-toe photo and look at it like it's someone else's

Photos flatten an outfit and give you distance. Look at the picture and ask what a stranger would notice first. If the answer is a wrinkle, a clashing color or a bunched waistband, that's what to fix.

Check the side and back, then sit, reach and walk

Turn sideways and look at the back. Then sit down, raise your arms and take a few steps. Check whether the shirt rides up, the waistband digs in, or the hem drags. These are the things other people see that you don't see head-on.

Photo tips (general photography advice)

These are general photography habits that tend to give a truer picture of an outfit, whatever camera or app you use:

  • Use even light and avoid strong backlighting.
  • Stand against a plain background where possible.
  • Hold the camera around waist or chest height, so legs aren't distorted.
  • Include your whole body and shoes, and skip filters.

A 7-point checklist to judge your outfit

Go through these in order. You don't need to pass every point perfectly; you're looking for the one or two things that pull the outfit down.

1. Fit

  • Shoulder seams on jackets and shirts should sit near the edge of your shoulder, unless the oversized look is deliberate.
  • Sleeves should end at the wrist on a fitted shirt, or look clearly intentional if rolled or cropped.
  • Trousers should hang cleanly. A small stack or slight break at the shoe is fine; puddling over the shoe usually looks unplanned.
  • Look for pulling across buttons, bunching at the waist, or gaping at the neckline.

2. Proportion

The easiest rule is to balance volume: pair something roomy with something more streamlined. An oversized sweater works well with slim or straight trousers. Wide-leg trousers usually look best with a fitted or tucked top. Also notice where hems and waistlines fall. A cropped jacket over a high-rise bottom looks deliberate, while a hem that stops at an awkward point on the leg can feel unplanned. If something feels off, try moving the hem or waistline slightly and compare.

3. Color

A reliable starting point is one neutral base plus two or three colors in total. Examples that rarely fail:

  • Navy trousers, white tee, tan shoes.
  • Olive pants, cream knit, brown boots.
  • Black jeans, grey sweater, one burgundy accessory.

Also check contrast. High contrast (black with white) looks sharp, while low contrast (beige with cream) looks soft. Neither is wrong, but a muddy middle, such as grey and washed-out navy, can read flat. If a color near your face looks dull on you, it can help to understand your skin tone depth and undertone, though this is a style preference, not a rule.

4. Texture, pattern and busyness

Aim for one focal point. If you have a bold print, keep everything else quiet. Mixing patterns can work when they differ in scale, such as a thin stripe with a large check, but stacking several loud things leads to the "too busy" feeling. Mixing textures, like denim with knit or leather with cotton, adds interest without adding noise.

5. Shoes and accessories

Shoes set the formality of the whole outfit. Clean white sneakers with tailored trousers read relaxed, while loafers or leather boots read polished. A belt, bag, watch or jewelry should either match the formality or add one small accent. If you're wearing three statement accessories, remove one.

6. Condition and grooming

Wrinkles, lint, scuffed shoes, loose threads and fraying hems cheapen an otherwise good outfit. Check that your hair is tidy in a way that suits the look. A quick steam or lint roll often does more than swapping a piece.

7. Occasion and comfort

Think about the dress code, the weather and what you'll be doing. Can you sit, walk and carry things? Will you be too warm or too cold? An outfit that fails here will look worse by mid-afternoon.

Why your outfit feels off: symptoms and quick fixes

When every piece is nice but the whole thing feels wrong, match the feeling to the likely cause below.

What it looks likeLikely causeQuick fix
Flat or boringEverything is the same tone or textureAdd contrast, a textured layer or one accent color
Messy or busyToo many colors or patterns competingCut back to a base neutral plus one focal piece
Boxy or shapelessVolume on top and bottom, no defined waistTuck or half-tuck, add a belt, or swap one piece for a closer fit
Formality mismatchDressy top with casual shoes, or the reverseChange the shoes or outer layer to match
SloppyWrinkles, scuffs, uneven hemsSteam or press, clean shoes, fix or swap the hem
Looks like a costumeEvery piece follows the same theme exactlyBreak up the theme with one neutral or contrasting item

Change one thing at a time and re-check. If you swap three items at once, you won't know which change helped.

Check your outfit for the occasion

Work and interviews

Lean slightly more polished than the everyday office standard. Neat, well-fitted pieces in solid or subtle colors, clean shoes and minimal accessories are a safe base. Check that everything is pressed.

Dates and evenings out

Choose something that suits the venue. A relaxed bar suits dark jeans, a good top and clean boots, while a formal restaurant suggests tailored trousers or a dress and dressier shoes. Pick an outfit you won't need to adjust all night.

Casual days and events

For casual plans, it's usually better to dress up one notch than down. A clean tee with a light jacket and tidy trainers looks considered, while the same tee with stained joggers rarely does.

When in doubt, read the venue

Check the event invitation, the venue's website or photos of other guests, and ask the host if you're unsure. The dress code is often hinted at in the details.

Getting a second opinion on your outfit

Ask a trusted friend specific questions

"Is it okay?" gets you a polite yes. Better questions are "Do these shoes fit the rest?", "Is the top too long with these trousers?" or "Which of these two is better for tonight?"

Compare two options side by side

Take photos of both outfits in the same light and place them next to each other. Differences you can't feel in the mirror often jump out in a direct comparison.

Use an AI outfit checker as one more opinion

If you're alone or don't want to ask anyone, an AI outfit checker can give you quick feedback on things like color match and balance. Treat it as a starting point rather than a verdict; it isn't a professional stylist and can't know your taste, your event or your comfort.

Taste is subjective

Rules of color and proportion are guidelines, not laws. If you love a combination that breaks them and you feel great in it, that counts for a lot.

  • Photo check: take or upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes, and you get an instant fit check and an AI outfit score.
  • Style breakdown: the feedback covers color match, proportion and overall balance, with what's working and easy ways to improve, such as switching shoes, adjusting color contrast or balancing the fit.
  • Live FitCheck: check an outfit live with the camera, with an outfit rating, color analysis, and matching and styling suggestions.
  • Digital closet: save your top-scoring looks so you can repeat outfits that worked.

Outfit scoring photos are processed directly on your device. The score is an AI opinion and a second opinion, not an objective measure or professional styling advice, so use it alongside your own judgment and the checklist above.

A 60-second final check before you head out

Screenshot this and run through it at the door:

  1. Shoes on, full-length mirror, good light.
  2. Does anything pull, gap, bunch or drag?
  3. Is there one neutral base and no more than two or three colors?
  4. Is there one focal point, not three?
  5. Do the shoes match the formality of the rest?
  6. Any wrinkles, lint, scuffs or loose threads?
  7. Can you sit, walk and reach comfortably, and is it right for the weather and the occasion?

faqs.answer: No. Guidelines like one neutral base plus two or three colors are useful when you're unsure, but they're not strict rules. If you like a combination and feel good wearing it, it works. Use the guidelines mainly to figure out why a look feels off.

how-to-organize-your-closet.body_html:
To organize your closet, take everything out, sort it into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season piles, group what stays by category, then store it so your most-worn pieces are the easiest to reach. Most of the work is deciding what earns a place, not buying containers. The steps below work for a walk-in, a small reach-in, or a closet you share.

Before you start: set a goal and block out the time

Decide what "organized" means for you. It might be faster mornings, more free space, or wearing more of what you already own. Your goal shapes your choices later. If you want faster mornings, for example, you will be stricter about pieces you never reach for.

Quick tidy or full reset?

A quick tidy (refolding, rehanging, removing obvious donations) can take under an hour. A full reset, where every item comes out, is better for a closet that feels overwhelming, and it usually needs a free half day. If you can't spare that, work one section at a time, such as shelves on Saturday and hanging clothes on Sunday.

What you need

  • Bags or boxes labeled donate, repair and out-of-season
  • A full-length mirror and good light
  • A clear floor or bed to lay things out on
  • Matching hangers, if you have them

Step 1: Take everything out (or one section at a time)

Seeing everything at once shows you duplicates, forgotten pieces and how much you actually own. If the closet is big, empty one zone at a time: all hanging tops, then bottoms, then shelves, then shoes. Once a section is empty, wipe down the shelves and rod and vacuum the floor before anything goes back in. A clean, empty space also helps you picture a better layout.

Step 2: Sort into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season

Pick up each piece and ask a few plain questions:

  • Does it fit now? Not "it might fit someday", but how it fits today.
  • Is it comfortable? If you keep adjusting it, you probably won't wear it.
  • Is it in good condition? Look for pilling, stretched necklines, stains, loose hems and missing buttons.
  • Do I have somewhere to wear it? A great jacket doesn't help if your life has no place for it.
  • Would I choose it again today? This question settles most borderline cases.

The try-on test for borderline pieces

If you can't decide, try the piece on in front of a mirror in good light, with the shoes you'd normally wear. Check whether it sits well on the shoulders, whether the length is where you want it, and whether the color looks good near your face. If you need a better understanding of which shades suit you, our guide to finding your skin tone depth and undertone can help.

Handle the "maybe" pile with a date

Put maybes in a box and write a review date on it, about three months out. If you haven't taken anything out of the box by then, donate it. This keeps you from getting stuck while sparing you the pressure of deciding on the spot.

Sentimental and "someday" clothes

You don't have to get rid of these, but they shouldn't take up prime hanging space. Give them one box or one shelf, kept apart from the clothes you wear every week.

Get donations and repairs out of the house

Put the donation bag in your car or by the door the same day. For repairs, set a deadline, for instance two weeks. Anything not mended by then goes to donation.

Step 3: Group what you're keeping

Start with category: tops, bottoms, dresses, outerwear, and so on. Within each category, sort by whatever fits how you dress:

  • Color: works well if you pick outfits by color. Go light to dark within each group.
  • Sleeve length or garment length: short sleeves before long sleeves, or shorter skirts before longer ones. This makes layering choices easier.
  • Occasion: if your life splits cleanly into work, casual, workout and event clothes, give each its own zone.

Category first, then color is the simplest default. Add the occasion split only if you really do dress in separate modes.

Step 4: Choose storage that suits your clothes and your space

Hang or fold?

Usually hang:

  • Blazers and coats
  • Dress shirts
  • Dresses
  • Trousers, especially if you want to keep a crease

Usually fold:

  • Knitwear and sweaters (hanging can stretch the shoulders)
  • T-shirts
  • Jeans
  • Workout clothes

Treat this as general guidance. Check care labels, and adjust for how much rod and shelf space you have.

Don't overcrowd

If you have to push hangers apart to see a garment, the rod is too full. Matching hangers keep the line tidy and make it easier to scan what you own. Leave a hand's width of room so clothes don't wrinkle against each other.

Shelves, drawers and bins

Fold knits and tees into stacks you can see from the side, so you don't need to dig. Use bins for like items (belts, scarves, gym gear), and use the vertical space above the rod for out-of-season or occasion items. Keep like with like, so there's always one obvious place for each thing.

Shoes, bags, belts, scarves and jewelry

  • Put everyday shoes at floor level or on a low rack, and rarely worn pairs higher up.
  • Hang belts and scarves on hooks or a slim hanger so you can see them all.
  • Stand bags upright (stuffed lightly so they hold their shape) rather than piling them.
  • Use a shallow tray or divided drawer for jewelry so pieces don't tangle.

Small or shared closets

In a small closet, use double-hang rods for shorter items like shirts and skirts, and move off-season clothes under the bed or on a top shelf. In a shared closet, divide it by side or by shelf, and keep a small overflow zone so neither person's clothes spill into the other's space.

Step 5: Place things by how often you wear them

Keep everyday pieces between shoulder and knee height, where you can reach them without bending or stretching. Move the rarely worn pieces higher or lower. This one rule makes a closet feel much easier to use.

Seasonal rotation

To organize clothes by season, store the pieces you won't need for a few months in labeled bins or garment bags. Clean everything before storing it. Swap at the change of season, and use the swap as your chance to reassess what you didn't wear last time. Leave transitional layers, like a light jacket or a cardigan, in the main closet all year.

Formalwear and occasion pieces

Suits, gowns and formal shoes should live together at one end of the rod, in breathable garment bags if possible, so they stay in good shape and are easy to find when needed.

Step 6: Turn a tidy closet into outfits you'll wear

An organized closet only pays off if it helps you get dressed. Spend ten minutes building three to five outfits from what you kept, and notice which pieces appear again and again.

Use simple outfit formulas

  • Smart casual: navy blazer + white tee + straight-leg jeans + white sneakers.
  • Relaxed layers: olive overshirt + cream tee + dark trousers + brown boots.
  • Balanced proportions: wide-leg trousers + fitted top, or an oversized sweater + slim trousers. Pairing loose with fitted usually works better than loose with loose, though an all-oversized look can be a deliberate choice.

Pairings that tend to work: camel with navy, charcoal with burgundy, cream with olive, and black with white or gray. Keeping a few neutrals as your base makes everything easier to mix.

Spot gaps before buying anything

If you keep building outfits that need a neutral layer, a versatile shoe, or a missing color, write it down. That list is far more useful than shopping without a plan, and it stops you from adding more things you won't wear.

A simple capsule approach

A capsule wardrobe closet is just a core of mix-and-match pieces in colors that work together. Choose two or three neutrals plus one or two accent colors, then check that most tops work with most bottoms. When you're unsure how to start your day, our 5-step guide to deciding what to wear today pairs well with a freshly organized closet.

How to keep your closet organized

  • One in, one out: when something new comes in, something leaves.
  • A 10-minute monthly reset: rehang, refold, and move anything out of place.
  • A twice-a-year review: do it at the seasonal swap and look for items you never wore.
  • Check the maybe box: on its review date, decide on everything inside it.

Where FitCheck AI can help (Android)

A physical closet still needs your hands, and no app will sort it for you. But once it's tidy, FitCheck AI can support the next step. Its digital closet and wardrobe organizer lets you organize clothes by season or occasion, save favorite and top-scoring looks, build a capsule wardrobe and plan outfits ahead for work, weekends or events.

If you're unsure about a borderline piece, you can also upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes and get an AI outfit score with a breakdown of color match, proportion and balance. Treat that as a second opinion, not a professional stylist's verdict or an objective answer. The app is free on Google Play for Android, and iOS is coming soon.

faqs.question: How often should I reorganize my closet?

faqs.answer: Start with type (tops, bottoms, dresses, outerwear), then arrange each group by color. This gives you a logical structure and a visual flow. If your life splits clearly into work and casual, add an occasion zone on top of that.
faqs.question: Should I organize my closet by color or by type?

faqs.answer: There's no universal number. Keep what fits, is in good condition and suits the way you actually live, and what you'd happily wear this month. If you can see and reach everything without cramming, you're probably in a good range.
faqs.question: How many clothes should I keep?

faqs.answer: Use stackable bins or a freestanding shelf unit on the floor, hanging organizers on the rod for folded items, and over-the-door hooks for bags and belts. Double-hanging rods can also help you use the vertical space.
faqs.question: What's the best way to organize a closet with no shelves?

faqs.answer: Follow a one-in, one-out rule, give every category a clear home, and do a short monthly reset. Messes usually come back when there's no obvious place for something, so adjust the layout if the same spot keeps filling up.

makeup-virtual-try-on-guide.body_html:
A makeup virtual try-on uses your phone camera to layer digital color, such as a lipstick shade, onto a live image of your face so you can preview a look before you apply anything. It works best as a quick way to compare colors and overall effect, not as a promise of how a specific product will look or wear. This guide covers how to get a realistic preview and how to turn it into a real-life decision.

What a makeup virtual try-on is (and what it isn't)

How a live camera preview works in plain terms

In general, these tools use your camera to find your face, then place a color over areas of the face. Which areas are supported depends on the tool. Because the preview is live, you can turn your head, smile and change expression to see how the color moves with you. Think of it as a mirror that lets you test ideas without a makeup bag.

What it's good for: color, placement and overall effect

A preview is useful for quick answers to questions like these:

  • Does a warm coral lip look balanced with my coloring, or does a cooler rose suit me better?
  • Does a bold lip feel too heavy, or does it feel like a polished finish?
  • Does the overall effect feel soft and everyday, or more dramatic?
  • Which of these two looks feels right for a work day versus an evening out?

What it can't show: texture, finish, wear and formula behavior

A screen can't reproduce how a product feels or behaves on skin. Use the table below to set your expectations.

A preview can help withA preview can't tell you
General color family and intensityExact shade or how a specific product will look
Placement and overall effectTexture, coverage and how a formula sits on your skin
Whether a look suits the occasionHow long it lasts or how it fades through the day
Comparing two or three ideas quicklyHow a color reads in every kind of light

Set up for a realistic preview

Face natural light and hold the camera at eye level

Stand facing a window so daylight falls evenly on your face. Hold the phone at eye level. A camera held low adds shadows under the chin and nose, and those shadows muddy lip colors.

Skip beauty filters and heavy retouching

Smoothing and brightening filters change your skin tone on screen, so any color you try on top will look different from real life. Turn them off to get the most honest view.

Start from a clean or neutral base so colors read clearly

If you're wearing heavy lipstick or bold eye makeup, the preview will blend with it. A bare or lightly done face gives the cleanest read of how a new color looks.

Check on more than one screen brightness

Screen brightness changes how saturated a color appears. Look at your favorite option at a medium and a high brightness. If it looks good at both, that is a good sign.

Before you try colors: know your starting point

Undertone and depth in one minute

Depth is how light or deep your skin is. Undertone is the cool, warm or neutral tint beneath the surface. As a loose starting point, cooler undertones often look balanced in berry, rose and blue-leaning pinks, while warmer undertones often suit coral, peach and terracotta. If you're unsure where you land, our guide on how to find your skin depth and undertone walks through it.

How contrast level changes what looks balanced

Contrast is the difference between your hair, skin and eye color. High contrast, such as dark hair with fair skin, can usually carry a defined lip like deep red or plum. Softer contrast, such as light brown hair with medium skin, often looks harmonious with softer tones like a muted rose or a brown-leaning nude.

Why this is a loose guide, not a rule

Plenty of people look great in colors that break these guidelines. Use undertone and contrast to choose what to try first, then let the preview and your own taste decide.

How to try makeup virtually, step by step

  1. Start with one change. A lip color is the easiest place to begin because it makes the biggest difference with the least guesswork.
  2. Compare a few shades side by side. Try something like a warm nude, a rosy pink and a deeper berry. Changing only one variable at a time makes it easier to see what you actually prefer.
  3. Look up close and at arm's length. Up close shows intensity. At arm's length you see how the look reads to other people.
  4. Think about the rest of the look. Once a lip works, picture what you'd wear with it, such as a cheek color in the same warm or cool family. Keep it simple, and note that which products you can preview depends on the tool you use.
  5. Keep a short list of your top two or three. Take a screenshot with your phone's own screenshot function, or jot down a description of each, such as "warm rosy-brown, medium intensity." A short list is much easier to act on than a pile of maybes.

How to judge a preview honestly

Does it suit your coloring, or just the lighting?

If a color only looks good under one lamp or at one angle, treat it with caution. Recheck near a window and see whether it still looks flattering.

Does the look match the occasion and your outfit?

A bold red lip can feel great with a simple black top and feel overwhelming with a busy print. Once you've settled on a look, you can also check how it sits with what you're wearing. The virtual outfit try-on feature shows AI-generated images of you in different outfits from your photo, which can help you picture the whole look together.

Does it feel like you, and is it easy to recreate?

A look you can't replicate on a regular morning isn't very useful. If a preview needs three products and a steady hand for winged liner, ask whether you'll really do that. A simple lip and cheek combination often wins for everyday wear. If you're still deciding which looks to try, our self-guided quiz on what makeup suits your face is a good place to start.

From screen to real life

Swatch-test before committing

Test the real product on your jawline or inner wrist in daylight. The jawline is closer to your face color, while the wrist is easier to compare several shades on at once.

Match finish and intensity to the preview

Decide what you liked in the preview: a sheer wash of color, a satin finish or a full-coverage matte. Then look for a formula that matches that effect. A sheer tint and an opaque matte can be the same color on screen and very different on your lips.

Use your favorite preview as a reference, not a shade promise

Show your screenshot to a friend or a beauty counter artist as a mood reference. Describe it in words too, for example: a warm rosy-brown, medium intensity, soft finish. That gives them something to work with, and you still get to see the real product on your skin.

Common reasons a preview looks different in person

Screen color and brightness settings

Phones display color differently, and night modes or warm-tone settings shift everything. A coral can look orange on one phone and pink on another.

Indoor lighting versus daylight

Warm indoor bulbs add yellow, which makes cool pinks look duller. Cool white lights can make warm shades look flat. This is why a daylight check matters.

Sheer versus opaque formulas

A preview usually shows one level of color, while real products range from sheer to fully opaque. Your natural lip color also shows through sheer formulas and changes the end result.

How FitCheck AI can help you try makeup virtually

FitCheck AI is an Android app with several features that fit this process:

  • Live virtual makeup try-on: preview makeup looks, such as lipstick, on your own face with the live camera.
  • Makeup assist with live camera guidance while you work on a look.
  • AI makeup assistant: personalized suggestions and feedback on makeup looks, from an everyday glow to full glam, based on your appearance.
  • Live skin analysis (optional): an AI overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. This is not medical advice.

Lipstick is the example of a live try-on look that the app confirms. This guide doesn't assume that other products, such as blush or eye makeup, or saving looks inside the app, are available. For the best result, follow the same photo advice as above: face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. The app is free on Google Play for Android, and iOS is coming soon.

Good to know

Previews and AI feedback are a second opinion and a starting point. They are not a substitute for a professional makeup artist, and the scores and suggestions are AI opinion rather than fact. Skin feedback here is cosmetic only. If you have any concern about your skin, such as irritation, breakouts or a changing mole, please see a dermatologist or doctor.

If you also want to experiment with your hair, the same approach works there: try hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut.

faqs.answer: No, and a clean or lightly done face usually gives the clearest result. Existing makeup mixes with the digital color and can hide what you're trying to see. If you already have lipstick on, remove it before you test new shades.

faqs.answer: Face a window so soft natural light falls evenly on your face, and hold the camera at eye level. Avoid strong overhead lights and warm lamps, which cast shadows or shift color. Turn off beauty filters too, since they change how your skin tone appears.

faqs.answer: Match each look to the occasion and the outfit you'll wear, then ask which one feels most like you and is easiest to recreate. Check both near a window and at arm's length. If it's still a tie, choose the simpler one for daily wear and keep the bolder one for special events.

try-hairstyles-on-your-face.body_html:
To try hairstyles on your face, take a clear, front-facing photo and preview styles on it. You can use an AI tool that generates a new hairstyle on your picture, or compare reference photos with your own. A preview is not a promise, because your real hair texture, density and growth patterns decide the final result. It is still an inexpensive way to rule styles in or out before anyone picks up the scissors.

Why previewing a hairstyle is worth doing before you cut

A shirt that doesn't work goes back in the closet, but a cut that misses can take months to grow out. Seeing a style on your own face, rather than on a model with different features, helps you notice things a reference photo can't show. Examples are how a fringe sits against your forehead or whether a jaw-length bob suits your jawline.

What a preview can and can't tell you

A preview is good for judging overall shape and proportion: length, where the hair ends, how much volume sits around the face, and whether a fringe or side part looks balanced on you. It is not good at predicting how your hair behaves. It can't know if your hair is fine, if you have a cowlick at the front hairline, or if your curls shrink when dry. Treat it as a visual sketch, not a blueprint.

Why a good photo matters more than the tool

Whatever you use, the input shapes the output. A dim, tilted, filtered selfie makes it hard to judge anything fairly. A clear, even, straight-on photo gives you something you can assess properly. That is why the photo steps come before any tool.

How to take a photo that gives a realistic preview

Natural light and eye-level camera

Face a window so daylight falls evenly on your face. Avoid overhead lighting or a window behind you, which creates shadows and a dark outline around your hair. Hold the camera at eye level. Shooting from below exaggerates the jaw and chin, and shooting from above makes the forehead look larger. Both change how a hairstyle appears to fit.

Skip filters and heavy edits

Beauty filters smooth and reshape your face, so any hairstyle is then judged against a face that isn't quite yours. Turn them off, including any "touch up" setting in your camera app.

Neutral expression, hair pulled back or flat, face fully visible

Keep a relaxed expression and make sure your forehead, ears, jawline and neck are visible. If your hair is long or covers your face, pull it back or flatten it so your actual head shape shows. Take off hats, and consider removing glasses for your first round so you see the hair without distractions.

Take a front shot and a slight angle

A straight-on photo shows symmetry and fringe. A shot turned slightly to the side shows how layers, volume and length look in profile, which is closer to how people see you day to day. Having both lets you check each style from two views.

Ways to try hairstyles on your face

Using an app that generates AI images from your photo

With this kind of app, you provide your photo and it generates an image of you with a new hairstyle. That lets you look at a bob, curtain bangs or a pixie on your own features before deciding whether to pursue it. Remember that the image is a visual idea, not a forecast of how the cut will fall on your hair.

Using reference photos and holding them next to your own

Collect three to five photos of the cut you like, ideally from people with a similar hair type, and view them next to your own photo. Look at hair density and texture in the reference, not just the shape. A blunt bob on thick, straight hair behaves very differently on fine, wavy hair.

Low-tech options: styling, clips, wigs or temporary tweaks

You can imitate some changes at home, though only roughly. Pin long hair up to get a loose sense of a shorter length, or sweep your hair into a different parting. Clip-in fringes and inexpensive wigs can give a feel for a new fringe or length, but fit and texture won't match a real cut.

How to try hairstyles on your face with FitCheck AI

Upload or take a clear photo

If you're on Android, FitCheck AI lets you try different hairstyles on your own face. The app generates AI images of you with a new hairstyle from your photo. For hair photos, the app's own tips are to face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. The other steps above, such as a neutral expression, hair pulled back and two angles, are general good practice rather than app requirements.

Generate a new hairstyle on your own face

Start with your clearest front photo and look at the generated image with the questions in the next section. Then compare it with the other styles you're considering, so you have more than one idea to weigh up.

Explore hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration

The app also offers hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, and a way to check how a look comes together. Use it to collect ideas, such as a curl pattern you'd like to try or a shade to show a colorist. The app is free on Google Play, and you can read more about how it works.

Use the result as a second opinion, not a verdict

The result is an AI-generated image and an AI second opinion. It is not a verdict or professional stylist advice, so use it to narrow down options and start a conversation with your hairdresser.

How to judge a preview honestly

Check length, fringe and parting against your features

Ask specific questions instead of "do I like it?":

  • Length: Where does the hair end relative to your jaw, shoulders or collarbone? A chin-length cut puts the focus near the jawline, while longer lengths draw the eye further down.
  • Fringe: Does it frame your eyes or sit heavily on them? Curtain bangs are generally more forgiving than a blunt, full fringe.
  • Parting: A center part emphasizes symmetry, and a side part adds softness and lift at the crown.

Consider your real hair texture, density and curl pattern

This is where previews are weakest. Thick hair can feel heavy in a one-length cut and often benefits from layers or texturizing done by a stylist. Curly hair shrinks when it dries, so a length that looks right in the preview may sit much higher on you. Straight hair holds sharp lines well, but a heavily layered look may need daily styling to get the volume shown. If your hair is fine, ask your stylist which lengths and cutting styles keep it looking full.

Compare several options side by side

Don't pick the most dramatic result by default. Put four or five previews side by side, for example in your phone's photo gallery. Rate each on how flattering it looks, how close it is to your natural hair, and how realistic it is for your lifestyle. The ones that do well on all three are the real contenders.

Think about daily styling time and maintenance

Sharp, short or blunt cuts usually need regular trims to keep their shape. Long layers are often lower maintenance, but textured hair may still need product. If you only have a few minutes each morning, a style that depends on blow-drying and a flat iron may not last long.

Face shape as a loose starting point

Common shapes and what styles tend to balance them

Face-shape advice is a useful starting point, not a rule. The general idea is to balance the widest and narrowest areas of your face.

Face shapeTypical featuresStyles often suggested
OvalLength slightly more than width, softly rounded jawMost styles work; choose by hair type and preference
RoundSimilar width and length, soft jawLong layers, side parts, volume at the crown
SquareStrong, angular jaw and a broad foreheadSoft waves, layers that fall past the jaw, side-swept fringe
HeartWider forehead, narrower chinChin-length bobs, volume in the lower half, curtain bangs
Long / oblongLength clearly more than widthFringe, face-framing layers, width at the sides
DiamondProminent cheekbones, narrower forehead and jawFringe, styles with fullness at the chin and forehead

Why proportions, hairline and features matter as much as shape

Two people with the same face shape can suit different cuts. Your forehead height and hairline affect how a fringe sits. Your neck length affects which lengths feel balanced, and features such as a prominent nose or large eyes influence which fringes and partings look right on you.

When to ignore the rules

If you love a cut that the "rules" say you shouldn't have, look at it in a preview and judge it for yourself. Styling, confidence and the way you wear the hair often matter more than the textbook match.

Turning a preview into a hairdresser brief

Describe length, layers, fringe and finish in plain words

Hairdressers work from specifics. Instead of "something like this but nicer," say something like: "Jaw-length, one length at the back, with soft face-framing layers at the front, a long side-swept fringe, and a natural, slightly tousled finish." Mention the parting and how much styling you are willing to do.

Bring two or three reference images, including the preview

Show your preview along with a couple of photos of the cut on real people with hair similar to yours. The preview shows how the style relates to your face, and the reference photos show how the cut is built and how it moves.

Ask what is realistic for your hair type

Ask directly: "Will this work with my texture and density?" and "How much of my morning routine will it change?" A good stylist will tell you what to adjust, such as a few more layers, a longer length or a different fringe, so the result suits your hair rather than only the picture.

Don't forget color, glasses and outfit balance

How hair color interacts with skin tone and clothing colors

Color changes the whole look, so think about it as its own decision, separate from the cut. As loose guidance, many people find warm shades such as copper, caramel and golden brown flatter warmer skin tones, and cooler shades such as ash browns suit cooler ones. Strong contrast between hair and skin looks bold, and shades closer to your natural color look more subtle. Whether a color works with the clothes you wear most is personal, so pick shades you like and then hold them up against your usual wardrobe colors. A colorist can advise on what is achievable from your starting shade.

Hairstyles with glasses, necklines and your usual aesthetic

Glasses and hair compete for attention around the face. A heavy fringe can cover the top edge of thick frames, while curtain bangs usually sit comfortably around them. Necklines matter too: a short cut or an updo shows off a V-neck or open collar, while longer layers can soften a crew neck or high collar. If your wardrobe leans minimal or polished, a sleek cut tends to fit it, and a relaxed, textured cut suits casual, layered looks. For the outfit side, FitCheck AI's outfit photo check looks at color match, proportion and overall balance, which you can use as a second opinion on your clothes.

Low-risk ways to ease into a big change

Start with a trim or added layers

If a preview of a significant change excites you but you're unsure, move toward it in steps. Ask for a few inches off or some face-framing layers first, then reassess after a few weeks. It's far easier to go shorter later than to regrow.

Test a new parting or styling method for a week

Switch your parting, try a different blow-dry direction or wear your hair half-up for a week. Notice how it feels each day. If you like the preview but find the styling annoying, that tells you something useful.

Plan the in-between stage if you are growing out or going shorter

Any change has an awkward phase. When growing out a fringe, clips or headbands can help you cope. When going shorter, consider booking a shaping trim a few weeks later to keep the cut looking intentional. Knowing this in advance makes it much easier to stick with a change you wanted.

what-haircut-looks-good-on-me.body_html:
The haircut that looks good on you works with your hair texture and density, suits your face and features, and fits the time you will really spend styling it. Face shape helps, but it is only one factor. This guide walks you through five steps to narrow your options to two or three cuts worth trying.

Why "what haircut will look good on me" has more than one answer

Face shape is a starting point, not a rule

Face shape charts are popular because they are simple. They give ideas about where volume, length and a fringe (bangs) might sit. But two people with the same face shape can look good in very different cuts, because their hair behaves differently. Treat shape as a hint, not a verdict.

The five things that actually shape the result

  • Hair texture: straight, wavy, curly or coily.
  • Density and strand thickness: how much hair you have and how fine or coarse each strand is.
  • Face shape and features: jaw, forehead, ears, neck length.
  • Growth patterns: hairline shape, cowlicks, parting direction.
  • Lifestyle: styling time, trim schedule, work or sport needs.

Step 1: Decide what you want the cut to do

Low-maintenance, polished, or statement look

Start with the goal. A low-maintenance cut looks fine when it air-dries. A polished cut usually needs a blow-dry, iron or product. A statement cut, such as a sharp bob or a very short crop, is chosen for the look, and upkeep comes second. Knowing which you want will rule out many of the photos you save.

How much time you will really spend styling

Be honest. If your mornings allow five minutes, a blunt bob that needs smoothing every day may frustrate you, while a layered cut that works with your natural wave may suit you better. Write down your realistic daily styling time before you look at references.

How often you are willing to get trims

Short, precise shapes like crops, tapers and blunt bobs usually lose their outline faster as they grow. Longer, layered or shaggy cuts tend to grow out more gently. If you only want a trim every few months, pick a cut that still looks fine when a little overgrown.

Step 2: Start with your hair type and density

Straight, wavy, curly or coily: how texture changes a cut

  • Straight: blunt lines and one-length cuts show clearly. Layers add movement but can look wispy on very fine hair.
  • Wavy: long layers and shags often work with the wave. A very short cut can spring up and look shorter than planned.
  • Curly: shape matters as much as length. Cuts are often designed around the curl pattern, allowing for shrinkage as curls dry.
  • Coily: rounded shapes, tapers and twist-friendly lengths can all work. Shrinkage can be significant, so a hairdresser experienced with your texture is valuable.

Fine vs. coarse strands and low vs. high density

Fine hair often looks fuller with a blunt edge, such as a chin- or collarbone-length cut. Thick, high-density hair can look heavy and may benefit from internal layers or weight removal. Strand thickness and density are separate: you can have fine strands and a lot of them.

Where our hair type quiz fits in

If you are not sure how to describe your texture, our hair type quiz can help you put a name to it. That makes finding reference photos and talking to a hairdresser much easier.

Step 3: Use your face shape as a loose guide

How to look at your face shape honestly

Pull your hair back, face a window or natural light, and take a straight-on photo at eye level. Compare the width of your forehead, cheekbones and jaw, and how long your face is relative to its width. Avoid angles from above or below, which distort proportions.

Common starting points for each shape

Face shapeCommonly suggested ideasOften worth a second thought
OvalMost lengths and fringes can workFew restrictions; choose by hair type and upkeep
RoundLayers that start below the cheekbones, a side-swept fringe, lengths past the chinHeavy volume at the sides at cheek level
SquareSoft layers, waves around the jaw, a side partA blunt cut that ends exactly at the jawline
HeartChin-length bobs, side-swept fringes, volume at or below the jawLots of volume on top that widens the forehead
LongA fringe, chin to shoulder lengths, volume at the sidesVery long, flat, center-parted hair
DiamondFringes, volume at forehead and chin, hair tucked behind the cheekbonesVolume that sits exactly at the cheekbones

These are style conventions, not rules. Plenty of people break them on purpose and love the result.

What to do if you sit between two shapes

Most people do. Read both rows, then pick the suggestions that overlap, such as a side-swept fringe or soft layers. Then let hair type and upkeep make the final call.

Step 4: Check the details that change how a cut sits

Forehead height, hairline shape and cowlicks

A high forehead can be framed with a curtain or side-swept fringe. A low hairline may suit a lighter fringe or a swept-back style. A strong cowlick at the front can push a fringe in an unexpected direction, so a hairdresser may suggest a side part or a longer, heavier fringe. Check your growth patterns when your hair is wet and flat.

Jawline, ears and neck length

A strong jaw can be echoed with a sharp bob or softened with layers. Neck length is a matter of taste: a cut that finishes above the shoulders or is swept up shows more of the neck, while a collarbone-length cut or longer bob covers more of it. Pick whichever look you prefer, because these are style conventions rather than rules. If you are unsure about your ears, a cut that sits just over them lets you cover or show them as you like.

Glasses and facial hair

  • Glasses: a heavy fringe can collide with thick frames, so consider a longer, side-swept fringe or one that stops above the brow line.
  • Facial hair: if you have a beard, think of the cut and beard as one shape. A fade that blends into the beard looks cohesive, while a very long top with a very short beard can feel unbalanced.

Length: what each does to your proportions

  • Cropped: highlights the face, eyes and jaw. It needs more frequent trims.
  • Chin-length: draws a horizontal line at the jaw, which can emphasize it. Good for fine hair that looks fuller with a blunt edge.
  • Shoulder-length: versatile, works tied up or down, and suits most textures.
  • Long: can add vertical length and softness, but may look heavy without layers if hair is thick.

Choosing a short cut: barbershop terms

Salons and barbershops often use different words for similar ideas, but cut names are not tied to gender. Anyone can ask for a bob, a taper or a fade. What matters is the length, shape and texture you describe. The terms below are common barbershop language and apply to any short cut.

  • Taper: the sides and back get gradually shorter, so the result looks neat but not stark. It is a good middle ground if you are unsure.
  • Fade: goes shorter and sharper at the sides, which puts more focus on the top and the jaw. It needs regular visits to stay crisp.
  • Textured crop: leaves length on top with a short fringe. It tends to suit straight or wavy hair and is easy to style with a little product.
  • Longer on top: a swept-back or side-parted style gives more options, but it needs more daily styling and works best when your hairline and cowlicks cooperate.

Match the sides to your beard (or lack of one), and decide how often you will really go to the barber, because the shorter the cut, the sooner it loses its shape.

Step 5: Build a shortlist of two or three cuts

Collect reference photos with a similar texture and density

Save six to ten photos of people whose hair is close to yours in texture and thickness. A photo of pin-straight, dense hair is a poor guide if yours is fine and wavy, however much you like it.

Spot what you like in a reference

For each photo, name what you like: the outline, the fringe, the layers, the length or the way it is styled. You may find you like a soft fringe across several photos, even though the cuts are quite different.

Pick one safe option, one moderate change and one bolder idea

For example, if you have long straight hair, your safe option could be a trim with face-framing layers, a moderate change a collarbone-length cut, and a bolder idea a chin-length bob. This gives you a clear range to compare and discuss.

Preview your shortlist before you cut

Take a clear, natural-light photo at eye level, with no filters

Face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and skip filters, so the preview starts from a clear photo of you as you look day to day.

How to try hairstyles on your own face with FitCheck AI

FitCheck AI is a free Android app on Google Play. It can generate AI images of you with a new hairstyle from your photo, so you can try hairstyles on your own face before you book. It also offers hairstyle recommendations, which are AI suggestions for hairstyles to consider, and a live hair analysis with the camera for hairstyle and hair color ideas. The hair analysis is cosmetic, not medical. Our guide to previewing a cut before you commit covers the preview process in more detail.

How to judge a preview honestly

A preview is an AI-generated image, not a promise of how your real hair will fall. It can give you a sense of shape, length and fringe direction, but it cannot account for your exact texture, cowlicks or how you style it. Use previews to compare your two or three options and decide which to discuss with a hairdresser.

How to brief your hairdresser

What to say

Describe the length (point to where it should end, such as the collarbone), the outline (blunt or softly layered), the fringe (none, curtain, side-swept), how much texture you want, and your daily routine. For example: "I air-dry most days and have five minutes to style. I want a collarbone-length cut with soft layers and a curtain fringe." Bring your reference photos and a preview image if you have one.

Questions to ask

  • Will this work with my hair type and density?
  • How will it look when I air-dry it, not just after a blow-dry?
  • How often will I need a trim to keep the shape?
  • How will it grow out?

What to do if you are unsure

Start conservative. Length can be taken off at your next visit, but it cannot be put back. Ask for a first cut that is one or two inches longer than your goal, then go shorter once you have seen how it sits and styles.

If you plan to change your color

Some cuts show color differently. Blunt cuts show solid color clearly, while layered or textured cuts suit highlights and soft blends. If you plan to change your color, mention it to your hairdresser before the cut so the two work together.

Good to know

AI previews and suggestions are a second opinion, not a professional stylist's view, and a hairdresser can see and feel your hair in person. This article is cosmetic style guidance and not medical advice. For any concern about your skin, scalp or hair, speak to a doctor or dermatologist.

what-is-my-hair-type-quiz.body_html:
Your hair type comes down to three separate traits: the shape your hair dries in (straight, wavy, curly or coily), how thick each strand is, and how much hair you have overall. This quiz walks you through each one with a simple check you can do at home, then turns your answers into styling and haircut direction. It takes about ten minutes and needs a mirror, daylight and a piece of sewing thread.

How this "what is my hair type" quiz works

Hair type, texture and density: what each word means

People use these words loosely, so here is how this guide uses them:

  • Pattern (often called hair type): the shape your hair forms as it dries, from straight to tightly coiled.
  • Strand thickness (often called texture): whether individual strands are fine, medium or coarse.
  • Density: how many strands grow from your scalp, which is low, medium or high.

Two people can both have wavy hair and need completely different cuts because one has fine, low-density strands and the other has coarse, high-density hair. That is why this quiz treats them as separate questions.

Why the labels are a starting point, not a verdict

The 1A to 4C system is an informal shorthand that stylists and hair communities use. It is not a scientific classification, and most people have more than one pattern on their head. Use your result to describe your hair and narrow down styles, not as a box you have to fit into.

Before you start: set up so your answers are accurate

Start with clean, product-free, air-dried hair

Wash your hair with your usual shampoo, skip stylers, and let it air-dry completely. Heat tools, gels, oils and humidity all change how hair looks, so a quiz taken on blow-dried or product-coated hair will mislead you. If you can, wait until you have not used heat for a day or two.

Check in natural light and look at several sections

Stand near a window and look at your front hairline, crown, sides and nape separately. Your hair often behaves differently in each area, and noting that now makes Question 2 easier.

Question 1: What shape does your hair dry in?

Look at the mid-lengths and ends of your dry hair, not the roots.

Straight: falls flat from root to tip

Your hair hangs without bending, apart from a slight flick at the ends. Straight hair shows sharp, blunt lines clearly, but it can struggle to hold curls without help.

Wavy: forms a loose S-shape

Your hair bends in gentle S-shapes, often starting a little below the roots. It sits between flat and curly, and it can look straighter when it is long and heavier.

Curly: forms defined spirals or ringlets

Your hair springs into spirals or ringlets, from loose loops to tight corkscrews. Curls often look shorter than they really are when dry, because the strand pulls up as it coils.

Coily: forms tight coils or zig-zag patterns

Your hair forms very tight coils, small springs or sharp zig-zag bends, and it may look much shorter than its stretched length. Many people with coily hair have a mix of coil sizes across the head.

Question 2: How tight is the curl or wave?

Wide, medium or tight pattern, and what 1A to 4C labels try to capture

The numbers match your Question 1 answer (1 is straight, 2 wavy, 3 curly, 4 coily). The letters describe how wide or tight the pattern is, with A being the loosest and C the tightest. Here is a rough way to place yourself:

  • Wide: loose waves or large loops, roughly A.
  • Medium: clear S-shapes or curls about the width of a marker barrel, roughly B.
  • Tight: small curls or coils, roughly C.

The marker comparison is only an approximate guide, and the boundaries between A, B and C are informal, so a near match is good enough.

Why you may have different patterns in different sections

It is common to have looser waves at the front and tighter curls at the nape, or straighter lengths with a curlier underlayer. Pick the pattern that covers most of your head and note any exceptions. You do not need a perfect letter and number.

Question 3: Are your strands fine, medium or coarse?

The single-strand check against a piece of sewing thread

Take one clean, dry strand and hold it next to a piece of ordinary sewing thread. A shed hair from your brush or clothing works well, so there is no need to pull one out.

  • Thinner than the thread: fine.
  • About the same: medium.
  • Thicker than the thread: coarse.

You can also roll the strand between your fingers. Fine strands are barely noticeable, while coarse ones feel distinct. Fine hair tends to go limp under heavy products, while coarse hair usually holds weight and shape well but can take longer to style.

Why strand thickness is not the same as how much hair you have

You can have fine strands and a lot of them, or coarse strands and only a few. Thickness describes the individual strand, and the next question covers how many strands there are.

Question 4: How dense is your hair?

The ponytail and scalp-visibility checks

Try two quick checks:

  1. Scalp visibility: part your dry hair in the middle. If your scalp shows clearly right away, density is likely lower. If you have to part carefully to see it, density is likely higher.
  2. Ponytail feel: gather your hair into a low ponytail. A slim ponytail that a hair tie wraps around several times suggests lower density. One that fills your hand and a tie wraps only once or twice suggests higher density.

Low, medium and high density in plain language

Low density means a slim ponytail and easy scalp visibility. Medium sits in between. High density means a full ponytail and a scalp that is hard to see. This is a style question only: it affects which cuts look full and how much volume a style gives you.

Question 5: How does your hair behave in humidity and after shampooing?

Frizz, shrinkage and how long a style holds

Over a day or two, and on a damp day if you can, notice what your hair does. Then pick the closest match:

  • Swells and frizzes in humidity (A): smoothing or anti-frizz styling usually helps.
  • Shrinks noticeably as it dries (B): plan cut length with shrinkage in mind.
  • Looks good after shampooing but flat by day two (C): lightweight products and some root lift help.
  • Looks much the same all day (D): you have more freedom with styles.

After shampooing, compare wash day with day two or three. Check whether your pattern shows clearly when freshly washed and air-dried, how much volume you have, and how long a style lasts. Hair that swells in humidity and hair that falls flat by lunchtime need different styling approaches, even if the pattern is the same.

What coloring, heat and chemical treatments can change in how your hair looks and behaves

Coloring, bleaching, smoothing treatments and regular heat styling can all change how your hair looks and behaves, including how well a curl or wave forms. If your answers do not match what you remember from years ago, treatments may be part of the reason. A hairdresser can tell you what they see in person.

Your results: what your answers add up to

A quick table: pattern + thickness + density to styling direction

Find the row closest to your Questions 1 to 4 answers, then add the direction for your Question 5 letter.

Your answersStyling direction
Straight, fine, low densityBlunt cuts and one-length bobs look fuller. Use lightweight products and avoid heavy layers.
Straight, coarse, high densityLong layers or internal layers remove bulk and add movement.
Wavy, fine to mediumSoft layers help waves show. Air-dry with light mousse or a lightweight cream.
Curly, medium to coarseShape the cut around the curl pattern. Moisture-focused styling and a diffuser can help definition.
Coily, any thicknessCuts that work with shrinkage and volume. Twist-outs, braid-outs and protective styles are popular options.
Q5 = A (frizz in humidity)Favor smoothing, anti-frizz styling and cuts that do not rely on a precise finish.
Q5 = B (shrinks as it dries)Ask your hairdresser to account for shrinkage when choosing length.
Q5 = C (flat by day two)Choose lighter cuts with some layers, and use texture spray or root-lift products.
Combination not listedStart with your pattern row, then adjust for thickness (fine: lighter, coarse: more shaping) and density (low: fuller, blunt lines, high: removing bulk).

Haircut and styling ideas for straight, wavy, curly and coily hair

  • Straight: a sleek blunt bob, a long one-length cut or curtain bangs. Texture spray adds grip.
  • Wavy: a shoulder-length cut with soft layers, or a shag if your hair is medium to thick.
  • Curly: a layered cut that keeps curls balanced rather than triangle-shaped. Ask your hairdresser how they cut curls, since some cut them dry.
  • Coily: a tapered cut, a rounded shape or a longer style that is stretched for versatility.

How to describe your hair to a hairdresser in one sentence

Combine your answers: "I have medium-width curls, fine strands and low density, and I want a cut that adds volume without losing length." Bring two or three reference photos of cuts you like on a similar pattern.

Common mix-ups and edge cases

Wavy or curly? How to decide when you are in between

If a section holds a clear S-shape but does not form a closed loop, call it wavy. If it spirals into loops once it is product-free and air-dried, call it curly. If your hair does both, you can describe it as wavy-curly. Hairdressers usually care more about how it behaves than which label you choose.

Why your hair may look different from season to season or after a cut or color

Humidity, a recent haircut, the weight of your length and color treatments can all change how your pattern appears. Retake the quiz if your hair seems to have changed noticeably, and always under the same conditions: clean, product-free and air-dried.

From hair type to a hairstyle you will actually wear

Use your result as a filter for hairstyle inspiration

Once you know your hair type, search for inspiration using your own terms, such as "fine wavy shoulder-length layers". Photos of hair similar to yours are far more useful than saved cuts that need a completely different pattern.

Preview a style on your own photo before booking

It helps to see a cut on your own face before you commit. Our guide on how to try hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut covers how to do this well. Choose styles that suit your pattern, since a look designed for straight hair may not hold on tight curls.

How FitCheck AI can help with hairstyle, curl and hair color ideas

FitCheck AI does not tell you your hair type, so use the quiz above for that. What it can do is help with the step afterwards. You can explore hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, and use live hair analysis with the camera for cosmetic hairstyle and hair color ideas. You can also try hairstyles on your own face with AI-generated images made from your photo. For best results, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. The feedback is a starting point, not a professional stylist's opinion, so take your favorite ideas to your hairdresser.

If you are rethinking your whole look, our what makeup suits my face quiz is a good companion to this one.

Not medical advice

This quiz is cosmetic and styling guidance only, and AI feedback is not medical advice, so please see a doctor or dermatologist for any scalp, shedding, thinning or other hair concerns.

what-is-my-skin-tone.body_html:
Your skin tone has two parts: depth (how light or deep your skin looks) and undertone (the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface). To work out yours, look at your bare face in natural daylight, name the depth first, then use a few simple checks (veins, jewelry, a white top) to narrow down the undertone. Treat the answer as a starting point for choosing clothes, makeup and hair color, not as a rule.

Skin tone vs. undertone: two different things

Many guides use "skin tone" to mean everything at once, which is why the advice gets confusing. It helps to split it in two.

Depth: how light or deep your skin looks

Depth is the easy part. It describes how light or dark your skin appears overall, usually in loose terms like fair, light, medium, tan or deep. Depth mostly affects how much contrast you can wear. Someone with deep skin and dark hair can often carry very bright or very pale colors, while someone with fair skin and light hair may find very dark shades heavy near the face.

Undertone: the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface

Undertone is the subtle hue under the surface color. Two people with the same depth can have different undertones, which is why the same foundation or lipstick can look right on one and off on the other.

  • Cool: a pink, rosy or bluish cast.
  • Warm: a yellow, peachy or golden cast.
  • Neutral: a balance of the two, with no clear lean either way.
  • Olive: a muted green-gold cast, often described as sitting between warm and neutral.

Why surface color changes but undertone usually stays consistent

Your surface color shifts with sun, season and even a flush after a workout. Undertone is the steadier background hue, which makes it a useful reference for fine-tuning shades once you have considered depth and contrast. It is still a judgment call by eye, which is why the checks below work best when you combine them.

Set up first: how to look at your skin properly

Most wrong answers come from bad viewing conditions, not bad tests. Spend two minutes on setup before you try anything.

Natural daylight, bare face, no filters

Stand by a window in daylight, ideally not in direct harsh sun. Remove makeup, tinted moisturizer and self-tanner if you can. Turn off camera filters and beauty modes, since they smooth and shift color. Warm bulbs add yellow and cool LEDs add blue, so skip indoor lighting for this.

Which areas to check (jawline, neck, inner arm) and why

Check a few spots rather than one. The jawline and neck are useful comparison points next to your cheeks, but necks are often sun-exposed too, so if your neck looks clearly darker or redder than the rest of your face, don't treat it as your baseline. The inner forearm is often more sheltered from sun than the backs of your hands, though this varies from person to person. If the spots look broadly similar in cast, that is a helpful sign.

Why tanning, redness and indoor lighting can mislead you

A recent tan can make you look warmer and deeper than your usual baseline. Temporary flushing from heat, exercise or a hot shower can make skin look pinker, which may push you toward guessing "cool." If either applies, check the more sheltered areas, or repeat your checks in a few days.

How to find your undertone at home

None of these tests is proof on its own. Run all three, note which way each leans, and look for the overall pattern.

The vein check: what it can and can't tell you

Look at the veins on the inside of your wrist in daylight. Veins that look more blue or purple often point cool, and veins that look more green often point warm. If you cannot tell, or see a mix, that can suggest neutral. This check is limited: depth, lighting and how visible your veins are all change what you see, so treat it as one clue.

The jewelry check: silver vs. gold

Hold a silver piece and a gold piece against your bare skin. If silver looks crisper and more flattering, that leans cool. If gold looks richer and warmer on you, that leans warm. If both look fine, you may be neutral. This is also about personal preference, since many people love the metal their undertone "doesn't" favor.

The white paper or white top check

Hold a plain white sheet of paper or a bright white top under your chin, then compare it with an off-white or cream one. Pure white may bring out pink in cooler undertones, while cream can look more harmonious on warmer ones. Pay attention to whether your face looks fresh or slightly washed out, not just to the color of your skin.

What 'neutral' and 'olive' mean, and why they're easy to mix up

Neutral means no strong lean; both warm and cool shades may work for you. Olive has a distinct muted green-gold cast, so it can look "off" in very pink or very orange shades but lovely in earthy tones. People often mistake olive for warm because of the yellow in it, but its greenish note makes some golden shades look sallow while others look rich. Try a few options side by side to see what feels right.

CheckLeans coolLeans warmMay be neutral or olive
Wrist veinsBlue or purpleGreenA mix, or hard to tell
JewelrySilver looks betterGold looks betterBoth work
White vs. cream topBright white looks freshCream looks softerBoth fine; or muted tones suit best

How to name your depth

Fair, light, medium, tan, deep: loose descriptions, not strict categories

Compare yourself to the people around you in the same daylight and pick the word that fits best: fair, light, medium, tan or deep. Brands and charts use different names and different numbers of steps, so your label in one place may not match another. That is normal. If you want a more structured vocabulary, the Monk Skin Tone Scale is one widely used 10-shade reference for depth. It is a depth reference, so you still need the undertone checks above.

Why a skin tone chart is a rough reference, not a verdict

A skin tone chart can give you a vocabulary, but screens display color differently, and no chart can account for the full range of human skin. Use it to get close, then rely on how colors look on you in person. Your final answer might be something like "medium depth, warm undertone" or "deep, neutral-cool," and that is plenty of detail to work with.

What to do with your skin tone and undertone

Clothing colors: working with contrast, neutrals and brights

Start with contrast level (your depth, plus how your hair and eyes compare to your skin), then adjust for undertone.

  • Warm undertones often look good in camel, olive green, rust, cream, warm red and mustard. Example: a cream knit, camel trousers and a rust scarf.
  • Cool undertones often look good in navy, charcoal, emerald, cool pink, plum and true white. Example: a navy blazer, white tee and gray trousers, with an emerald top for a bolder look.
  • Neutral undertones usually have the most flexibility, so try both sides and pick by mood.
  • Olive undertones often suit earthy and jewel shades like forest green, burgundy, terracotta and warm taupe. Try them next to your face before committing to very pastel or neon options.

Colors worn near your face matter most, so test a top or scarf at the neckline. For lower-body pieces, wear whatever you like. If you want to see how colors work together in a full outfit, Live FitCheck can check an outfit live with the camera and give color analysis, matching and styling suggestions. Treat those suggestions as one opinion to weigh, not a final verdict.

Makeup: testing foundation on the jawline in daylight

To find a foundation shade, swatch two or three close options along the jawline, not the back of your hand, and check them in daylight. The right one tends to blend into your neck without a visible line. Then consider undertone: a shade that looks slightly gray on you may be too cool, and one that looks yellow or orange may be too warm. For blush and lip, warm undertones often like peach, coral and terracotta, while cool undertones often like rose, berry and cool pink. Neutral and olive skin can usually go either way, so try both. To preview a lip color before you buy it, FitCheck AI's live virtual makeup try-on lets you see looks such as lipstick on your own face through the live camera.

Hair color and jewelry metals: general starting points

Warm undertones often pair well with golden blonde, honey, copper and warm brown, plus gold jewelry. Cool undertones often pair well with ash tones, espresso, blue-black and silver jewelry. Neutral skin can wear mixed metals easily. These are widely used starting points, not requirements. If you are weighing a bigger change, previewing it first helps; our guide on trying hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut covers how.

When to break the rules: taste, occasion and personality

Undertone guidance is a shortcut for finding colors that flatter you, but it will not tell you what you enjoy wearing. A color that is "wrong" for your undertone can still work if you keep it away from your face, add a scarf or necklace in a better shade, or simply love it. Occasion matters too: a uniform, a wedding palette or a dress code often outranks any color rule.

Where a camera-based tool fits in

What FitCheck's live skin analysis does

FitCheck AI's live skin analysis uses the camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. It is not a skin tone or undertone test, so keep using the daylight checks above to work out your depth and undertone. If you are curious about cosmetic suggestions for your look, you can weigh them alongside what you see yourself. The app is available on Android (free on Google Play), and an iOS version is coming soon.

Photo tips: natural light, eye level, no filters

For makeup and beauty features, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and turn off any filters.

Why AI feedback is a starting point, not a professional color analysis

AI feedback is an opinion, not a measurement, and it is not a professional stylist or a formal color analysis. Use it as one input alongside your own checks and your own sense of what looks and feels like you.

Not medical advice

This guide is about cosmetic style only

Everything here is about color, makeup and style choices. It does not diagnose, detect or treat anything about your skin, and it cannot tell you anything about skin health.

See a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern or change

AI feedback, including from skin analysis tools, is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern or change you notice.

faqs.answer: Your surface color can shift with the seasons, sun exposure and the way your skin looks day to day, so your depth may look lighter or deeper at different times. Undertone is generally steadier, though perception can change with a tan or temporary flush. If you are unsure, re-check in daylight on a sheltered area like your inner arm.
faqs.question: Can my skin tone change over time?

faqs.answer: That is common, because warm bulbs, cool LEDs and filters all push color around. Trust natural daylight over indoor lighting, and repeat your checks at a window at a different time of day. If results still conflict, you may simply be neutral, and a flexible color palette will serve you well.
faqs.question: What if my results are different in different lights?

faqs.answer: This often points to a neutral undertone, which gives you the most room to experiment. Pick colors by what you like and the mood you want, and test them at the neckline. You can also lean on contrast and depth, which often matter as much as undertone.
faqs.question: What if I seem to fit both warm and cool?

faqs.answer: No. Undertone is a helpful shortcut, not a requirement. If you love a shade that isn't the textbook match, wear it away from your face, pair it with a flattering color near your neckline, or just enjoy it.
